title: Survival Analysis
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of survival analysis and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply time-to-event data in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Survival Analysis is part of Specialized R Domains. Start with time-to-event data and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Specialist methods carry domain-specific data requirements and assumptions; choosing a package does not replace subject-matter validation.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Specialist methods carry domain-specific data requirements and assumptions; choosing a package does not replace subject-matter validation. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Time-to-Event Data
items.text: For time-to-event data, parse values to a date-time class first and verify formats, timezone assumptions and a boundary date.

items.title: Censoring
items.text: Explain censoring in the context of survival analysis, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Kaplan–Meier Estimation
items.text: Explain kaplan–meier estimation in the context of survival analysis, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Log-Rank Tests
items.text: Explain log-rank tests in the context of survival analysis, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Cox Proportional Hazards Models
items.text: For cox proportional hazards models, state the statistical question and assumptions first, then describe the estimate or diagnostic in context.

items.title: Survival Model Diagnostics
items.text: Turn survival model diagnostics into a check with a clear condition, expected result and an example that should fail.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Name the domain assumptions, inspect the input schema and define a diagnostic or sensitivity check before interpretation. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Survival Analysis
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 233: Survival Analysis
specialist_input <- c(4, 5, 7)
summary(specialist_input)
content_blocks.expected_output: R prints a six-number summary for the synthetic numeric vector.

content_blocks.limitations: Specialist methods need domain-specific data, assumptions and diagnostics; this is only a generic input-inspection example. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For survival analysis, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
